title: FoundationDB, CockroachDB or TiDB?

rows.label: In one line
values: A distributed, ordered key-value store with strictly serializable transactions, meant as a base for other databases
A distributed SQL database that speaks the PostgreSQL wire protocol, with every node doing everything
A distributed SQL database that speaks the MySQL protocol, split into SQL, storage and coordination services

rows.label: What you talk to
values: Client libraries (C, Python, Java, Go and others) that read and write keys inside transactions; no query language, schema or secondary indexes in the core
SQL from `psql` and PostgreSQL drivers and ORMs, through any node
SQL from MySQL clients, drivers and ORMs, through stateless TiDB servers behind a load balancer

rows.label: SQL
values: Only through layers, such as the FoundationDB Record Layer’s SQL interface over JDBC
PostgreSQL-compatible, with gaps: no range types, foreign data wrappers or column-level privileges
Compatible with common MySQL 5.7 and 8.0 syntax, but no stored procedures, triggers, events or user-defined functions

rows.label: How the cluster is built
values: Separate roles: coordinators, a cluster controller, a sequencer, proxies, resolvers, transaction logs and storage servers, scaled independently
One `cockroach` binary per node; each node runs the SQL layer and stores replicas of some ranges
TiDB servers for SQL, Placement Driver (PD) for metadata and timestamps, TiKV for row storage, optional TiFlash for columns

rows.label: Replication
values: Commits are fsynced by the transaction logs, then pulled by storage servers; on failure the cluster recruits a new transaction system rather than voting
Raft per range of up to 512 MiB, three replicas by default; a leaseholder serves reads and coordinates writes
Raft per Region of 256 MiB by default in TiKV, three replicas; TiFlash copies data as asynchronous Raft learners

rows.label: Ordering transactions
values: A single sequencer hands out read and commit versions
Hybrid logical clocks over NTP; a node whose clock drifts past the maximum offset (500 ms) shuts itself down
A central timestamp oracle (TSO) in PD: a physical millisecond time plus a logical counter, per transaction

rows.label: Concurrency control
values: Optimistic: resolvers check the read set at commit, and a conflicting transaction fails with `not_committed` and is retried by the client
MVCC with serializable checks; conflicts surface as retry errors (SQLSTATE `40001`) the application must handle, unless the transaction arrives as one batch
MVCC with a Percolator-style two-phase commit; pessimistic locking by default since v3.0.8, optimistic mode available

rows.label: Default isolation
values: Strict serializability for every transaction
`SERIALIZABLE`; `READ COMMITTED` since 23.2
Snapshot isolation, reported as `REPEATABLE READ`, which allows write skew; `READ COMMITTED` in pessimistic mode

rows.label: Analytics
values: None built in; range reads over ordered keys
Row store; changefeeds stream changes to Kafka, Pub/Sub, cloud storage or webhooks for analysis elsewhere
TiFlash column replicas answer analytical queries on the same data, with snapshot-consistent reads

rows.label: Hard limits and gotchas
values: Transactions last at most 5 seconds and touch at most 10 MB; keys up to 10 KB, values up to 100 KB; no access control
Retry loops for `40001`; cross-region writes pay quorum round trips; licence key and telemetry needed for free production use
Transactions up to 100 MB by default (configurable to 1 TB) and rows up to 6 MiB; every transaction asks PD for timestamps; no spatial indexes and limited FULLTEXT

rows.label: Licence
values: Apache 2.0, maintained by Apple
Proprietary CockroachDB Software License since v24.3 (November 2024); free Enterprise for businesses under $10 million revenue
Apache 2.0, maintained by PingCAP

tip: These sit at different levels. FoundationDB is the transactional engine you build a database on, as Apple and Snowflake did; pick it only if you’re writing that layer yourself and can live with 5-second transactions. Between the two SQL databases, start from the protocol your applications already speak: TiDB for MySQL, CockroachDB for PostgreSQL. CockroachDB gives serializable isolation by default and runs as one binary that is easy to spread across regions, but it is no longer open source. TiDB is Apache 2.0, separates SQL, storage and analytics so each can scale on its own, and adds column replicas for reporting, at the cost of more components to run and weaker default isolation.
